findings: getDashboard awaits fetchLivePrice sequentially inside a for-loop instead of running the calls concurrently (e.g. Promise.all), so total request latency scales linearly with the number of orders on that account — this is the direct mechanism behind 'slow under load.'

pricingApi.get is called with no timeout configured (explicitly flagged in the code comment), so a single slow or hung downstream response blocks the entire dashboard request indefinitely with no upper bound on latency.

fetchLivePrice's catch block retries on ANY error with no distinction between transient and permanent failures (e.g. a genuinely invalid SKU or a 4xx-class error), so a permanent error causes retries that can never succeed.

The retry has no maximum attempt count and no backoff/delay — a failing pricingApi is hit with immediate, unbounded, back-to-back retries as fast as the network allows, rather than failing fast or backing off.

Because retries are immediate, unbounded, and issued per-order across every concurrent dashboard request, any degradation in pricingApi increases retry volume against it, which further degrades pricingApi — a self-reinforcing retry storm that plausibly explains the 'performance cascade' and full timeouts under load described in the scenario.

There is no circuit breaker or fallback path: fetchLivePrice only ever hangs/retries or eventually succeeds, so getDashboard has no way to return a partial or degraded response (e.g. omit price, use a cached value) when pricing is unavailable.

Because the loop is sequential (finding 1) and fetchLivePrice can retry indefinitely (findings 3-4), a single bad SKU or a single pricingApi hiccup on one order is sufficient to hang the entire response for a user, regardless of how many of their other orders would have resolved fine.
